sermon:
A man writes near the end of a long life and reaches first for his hands. Not for an argument, not for a doctrine, but for what his fingers once held. "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life" (1 John 1:1). John is an old man now, the last of the eyewitnesses, and false teachers have begun to whisper that the eternal Word never really took on flesh, never truly suffered, was too holy to be touched. So John leads with his body. He heard the voice. He saw the face. He put his hand on the side that bled.

**The Life That Appeared**

The opening sentence has no main verb until verse three, because John cannot finish the thought without circling back to what he touched. The life was made manifest, he says, and we have seen it and testify to it. This is the center of everything that follows. Eternal life is not a concept the apostles deduced. It is a person they buried and saw again. And the reason John tells us is plain: "so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ" (1:3). The eyewitness writes so that those who never touched can still belong. His hands stand in for ours.

Then comes the test of whether that fellowship is real. "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1:5). Light does not negotiate with the dark. It exposes it. So John names three lies people tell to keep fellowship cheap. If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar. Notice that all three are claims of innocence. The thing that keeps a person out of the light is not the sin itself. It is the pretending.

**The Confession That Cleanses**

Against the pretending stands one verb, repeated, almost stubborn. Confess. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1:9). Faithful, because he promised. Just, because the debt was actually paid. This is not God lowering the standard. This is God meeting it. And John tells us where the payment landed: Jesus Christ the righteous is our advocate before the Father, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only but for the whole world.

I have stood in pulpits and managed my own image so carefully that I called the managing humility. I have confessed in the abstract, sins in general, a vague and tidy guilt that costs nothing to admit. That is not walking in the light. That is decorating the dark. The man who says he has no sin has simply moved his sin somewhere the light cannot reach, and called the room clean. I have built that room. So have you.

**The Christ Connection**

Walking in the light is not walking sinlessly. It is walking honestly, in the company of the One who bled. The blood of Jesus his Son keeps cleansing us, present tense, ongoing, as we keep coming into the open. Christ is both the light that exposes and the advocate who answers when we are exposed. He does not stand at the door of fellowship demanding our innocence. He stands inside it, holding his own wounds, pleading our case. The hands John touched are the hands now raised for us.

So stop defending the version of yourself that has no sin. He never died for that man. That man does not exist. Come into the light where the blood is, and be cleansed.

Walk in the light. Confess.

Everyone wants to know if they are the real thing. The question hides under our certainties and surfaces at three in the morning. Do I actually know God, or have I only learned the language of people who do. John does not leave us to guess. He gives a test we can run on ourselves, and the test is not how we feel. "By this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments" (1 John 2:3).

**Knowing Shown by Keeping**

John is blunt about the alternative. Whoever says "I know him" but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. That is hard, and it is meant to be. Knowing God, in John's grammar, is not a private warmth. It produces a life that bends toward obedience, and where there is no bending, there is no knowing, whatever the mouth claims. Then he says something that sounds like a contradiction. He gives no new commandment, and yet he gives a new one. The old command is love, as old as Sinai. What is new is that it has been lived out in a single life, fully, for the first time, in Jesus, and now in those who abide in him. The darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But love has a measure, and the measure is your brother. "Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness" (2:9). You cannot stand in the light and resent the person beside you in it. John will not let love stay a feeling about humanity in general. He drives it to the particular person you find hard to forgive. The one who loves his brother abides in the light. The one who hates is in darkness and walks blind, not knowing where he goes.

**The Love That Cannot Hold the World**

Then John turns to the rival. "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (2:15). He is not talking about creation or about people. He defines his terms: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life. Appetite, acquisition, and applause. These are not in the world by accident. They are the architecture of a life built without God, and they cannot share a heart with the Father. A heart has one throne.

And here is the verdict that should sober anyone who has spent their best years chasing the next thing: "the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever" (2:17). The world is not merely dangerous. It is dying. To love it is to pour yourself into something already leaving.

I preach against worldliness easily, and then I check how a post performed, how a room received me, what I am owed. The pride of life is not somebody else's sin. It is the one that wears my collar. I have wanted God and the applause both, and John tells me the love of the Father is simply not in a heart arranged that way. I cannot keep both. Neither can you.

**The Christ Connection**

Why obey, why turn from the world. Not to earn a standing John says we already have. He writes to little children whose sins are forgiven for his name's sake, who have known the Father, in whom the word of God abides. The anointing they received remains, and teaches them, and is true. We love the Father not to become his children but because, in Christ, we already are. The cross did not buy us a probation. It bought us a home that does not pass away. To go on loving the dying world is to behave like an orphan after the adoption is final.

So look at what you reach for first in the quiet, before duty wakes. That is what you love. And whatever it is, if it is the world, it is already leaving you.

Love the Father, not the world.

Stand at a window and watch a father with his child, the way the man's whole face reorganizes around that small life. John reaches for that exact astonishment and then insists we take it personally. "See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are" (1 John 3:1). Not called as a courtesy. So we are. The verse almost stops to catch its breath at the word.

**Children Now, and Not Yet**

John holds two times at once. Now we are children of God. And what we will be has not yet appeared. The future is hidden, but its shape is sure: "we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is" (3:2). We become like what we behold, and one day we will behold him without a veil. Then John adds the present consequence: everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, as he is pure. The future does not make us passive. It makes us clean. Hope is not waiting. Hope is the slow scrubbing of a life pointed at a coming face.

So the children of God are recognizable. John says it plainly, without softening: whoever makes a practice of sinning practices lawlessness, and whoever has been born of God does not keep on sinning, because God's seed abides in him. This is not a claim of sinlessness; John already told us we have an advocate. It is a claim about direction. A child carries the family likeness. The one fathered by God cannot settle comfortably into the family business of sin, because a new life has been planted that will not let him.

**Love That Costs Something**

Then John names the family likeness with one word, and gives it a price. The message from the beginning is that we love one another, not as Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. Why did he kill him. Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous. Hatred and love both run in the blood from the very first brothers, and John makes us choose our line.

Here is the definition, and it is not sentimental: "By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers" (3:16). Love is measured at the cross and then handed to us as a debt. And lest we escape into the heroic abstraction of dying for someone, John drags it back to the ordinary. If anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him. Then the verse that judges all my fine words: "Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth" (3:18).

I am fluent in the word and talk of love. I can write about it, preach it, post it. And I have looked at a real need with a real name and felt my heart quietly close, calculating, protecting, moving on. John does not let me grade myself on the sermon. He grades me on the open hand or the shut one. Love that costs nothing is not a smaller love. It is a counterfeit.

**The Christ Connection**

Everything here flows from one act. He laid down his life for us. We did not first love and earn the title of children. He gave himself while we were Cain, while our deeds were evil, and made us sons by his own blood. The love we owe our brother is not generated by our goodness. It is the overflow of a love that reached us at the cross and now has to go somewhere. And when our hearts condemn us, John says, God is greater than our hearts. The Father who gave his Son does not now stand over us with a ledger. He stands behind us with his Spirit, whom he has given us.

So find the one real need you have been managing at a distance, and close the distance.

Love in deed and truth.

Not every voice claiming the Spirit is sent by him. John knew this in his own city, where teachers spoke with confidence and warmth and conviction, and led people quietly away from the Christ who came in flesh. So he refuses to let sincerity stand in for truth. "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1). Discernment is not suspicion. It is love guarding the door.

**Test the Spirits**

The test is narrow on purpose. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist. John does not test by power or eloquence or how a message makes the room feel. He tests by the body of Jesus. Did the Word actually become flesh, actually bleed, actually die. A spirit that floats above the incarnation, that prefers a Christ too spiritual to suffer, is not the Holy Spirit, however moving it sounds. Then John gives the assurance: little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.

Having drawn the line, John walks across it into the deep end. The God who came in flesh is love, and he says it twice so we cannot file it as one attribute among others. "Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love" (4:8). This is not the sentimental slogan the phrase has become. John defines it by an event. Love is not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. God is love, and the proof is a Son sent to absorb wrath. Strip the cross out of "God is love" and you have a different god, a softer one, and a lie.

**Because He First Loved**

So our love is never the origin of anything. "We love because he first loved us" (4:19). Every genuine affection in a Christian is a reflected light. He moved first, at the cross, before we wanted him, and our love is the answer the propitiation creates in us. John then closes every exit. If anyone says "I love God" and hates his brother, he is a liar. For the one who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. The brother is the visible test of the invisible claim. You cannot pass an unseen exam while failing the one in front of you.

I confess I find God easier to love than people, and now I see why. God whom I have not seen does not interrupt my morning, does not disappoint me, does not need anything from me at an inconvenient hour. The brother does. And John says the love I claim upward is measured by the love I refuse sideways. The convenient love is the counterfeit. The God I say I adore sent his Son into the flesh precisely to be inconvenienced unto death, and I want a love that costs me a feeling and not an evening. He calls that a lie, and names me the liar.

**The Christ Connection**

Here is what casts out the fear underneath all our self-protection. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. The propitiation already happened. The wrath I dread fell on the Son and is spent. I do not love in order to be safe. I am already safe, and so I can finally love without using people to secure myself. The cross is both the proof that God is love and the reason I have nothing left to fear, and a person with nothing to fear can spend himself freely on a brother.

So stop testing your love by your feelings about God, and test it by your open door to the brother who needs in.

We love because he first loved.

John has spent four chapters testing us, and a person could finish them unsure whether they belong. So he writes a fifth, and the whole weight of it falls on one word: know. Not hope, not feel, not hope so. "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). The letter that tested so hard was never meant to leave us anxious. It was meant to leave us certain.

**The Faith That Overcomes**

John ties faith and family together at the start. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him. The believing and the loving and the obeying are not separate achievements. They are one new life from one new birth. And this life is at war with the world, but the outcome is already settled. "For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith" (5:4). Notice the tense. Has overcome. The decisive battle is behind us, not ahead. Faith does not promise we will win someday. It connects us to the One who already won.

Then John appeals to evidence, because faith is not a feeling without grounds. He calls witnesses: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and they agree. God testifies to his Son, and whoever believes has the testimony in himself. The point is sober: "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life" (5:12). There is no life stored somewhere apart from Christ, no eternal life on deposit outside the Son. He is not the path to the life. He is the life. You either have him, and therefore have it, or you do not.

**The Knowledge of Eternal Life**

So John writes the whole letter for this: that you may know. And he extends the knowing into the place where we feel most uncertain, our prayers. This is the confidence we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us. Certainty about our standing produces boldness at the throne. The same assurance loosens our grip on fear, and three times in the closing John says we know. We know that everyone born of God does not keep on sinning, but the One born of God protects him. We know that we are from God. We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know him who is true.

I have lived too much of my ministry on hope so, treating assurance as presumption and doubt as humility. But John calls the not-knowing a failure to believe the testimony God himself has given. To shrug at my standing is not modesty. It is, quietly, calling God a liar about his own Son. I have done that, dressed it up as caution, and starved myself of the very confidence John bled to give me. So have many in our pews who have decided that uncertainty is the holiest posture available. It is not. It is unbelief with good manners.

**The Christ Connection**

All the knowing rests on one fact outside ourselves. The Son of God has come. The life is in him, not in the steadiness of our faith or the heat of our feelings. My assurance does not stand on how well I have loved my brother or kept the commandments; those are evidences, not the foundation. The foundation is that he came, he is the true God and eternal life, and he holds me so that the evil one does not touch me. I do not keep my grip on him. He keeps his grip on me. That is why I can know. And John ends the letter abruptly, almost like a father at a door: little children, keep yourselves from idols. Anything you put in the place of the Son will rob you of the certainty only the Son can give.

So stop offering God your uncertainty as if it were reverence. Take him at his word about his Son.

Know that you have life.
